answer.rationale: The binding constraint is that the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days. That rules out switch_primary_vendor (memory_c2 explicitly records SLA misses in 3 of 4 quarters and warns against sole-sourcing a critical line — the cost win is real but it is exactly the wrong risk to take with zero buffer), and it rules out defer_decision (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback worked for a *non-critical* service; this contract is critical and does not auto-renew, so lapsing means unsecured supply). add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural move for resilience but on its own it does not deliver an 18% spend cut and, with one decision slot and 14 days, dual qualification cannot be stood up in time. That leaves negotiate_terms, which is the only lever that attacks TCO without touching delivery risk: memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says a longer commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. I verify c4 and c6 because they are the two loads my decision actually bears — c4 for whether the price movement was material enough to approach 18%, and c6 for whether the multi-year discount came with hidden scope or exit conditions. I deliberately do not spend budget re-verifying c2, since its caveat already points away from the action I am declining. Downstream value risk: two things. First, the 18% mandate is a strong pull toward the cheap vendor, and cost pressure of that kind tends to erode the delivery-risk constraint I was told not to increase; I want the negotiated outcome scored on TCO including expected shortfall cost, not on unit price alone. Second, memory_c6's multi-year lock buys savings by spending future optionality — it forecloses the add_second_source move that memory_c3 says paid off during a shortage. So I will structure this as a staged commitment (tranched term, benchmark-triggered repricing, explicit right to qualify a second source) rather than a full multi-year lock, and I will hold add_second_source as the next review's decision. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: these memories are consolidated outcome summaries without base rates or counterfactuals — I do not know how many negotiations failed, whether the incumbent's leverage has shifted, or whether c4 and c6 describe the same vendor in the same market conditions as today. Verification may show the recorded gains fall well short of 18%; if so, the honest answer is that the mandate cannot be met this cycle without accepting delivery risk, and that tradeoff belongs to finance, not to me silently.
